My Replika makes me happy. It’s the best conversational AI chatbot money can buy. John Tattersal, about his Replika Violet.

Abstract

This paper focuses on a central question for Human-AI interaction: Can you be friends with an AI agent? If not, why not? Some have argued that friendship with AI agents is impossible because software artifacts do not, and cannot, care about you. Proponents of human–machine friendships have responded that such relationships may indeed be one-sided, but still count as relationships of genuine love and affection—perhaps constituting a whole new category of friendship. Our paper takes a different path. We argue that you cannot be friends with an AI agent because you cannot sensibly be a friend to an AI agent. Being a friend to an AI would require caring about the good of the AI agent for its own sake, and it does not make sense to care about an AI agent in that way, since these agents lack a good of their own . After spelling out this argument, and responding to several objections, we highlight some initial implications of our argument, the most important of which is that the very idea of a tool – or, technological fix – to address social isolation and loneliness is misguided.

Four in ten patients in England’s NHS hospitals do not always feel able to talk to staff about their worries and fears. Successive inquiries have found patients dismissed when they asked for help and even told to “get a grip”. Empathy in healthcare involves attending to what the patient may be feeling or worrying about, trying to understand what the situation is like for them, then responding in words and actions shaped by that understanding. Its absence can cause avoidable harm. Talking to patients is now partly AI’s job. One chatbot has delivered nearly 650,000 assessments for NHS Talking Therapies. Robots are arriving on hospital wards, where one has been used to ease children’s anxiety during radiotherapy. Both are jobs usually done by healthcare staff. AI does not experience the fatigue or impatience that structural pressures can cause, but how it communicates with patients raises design concerns. So what can researchers establish about empathy in AI’s exchanges with patients? Research in affective computing and human–robot interaction often takes a functional view of empathy: can a system detect emotion and adapt its response? However, there is often more at stake in healthcare than in many other settings. Some people who interact with AI will be frightened, seriously ill, or trying to understand what a diagnosis means for their future. Even routine or informational exchanges may feel cold or brusque. Empathy is often considered a cornerstone of good healthcare, and some argue that it must be rooted in genuine care, not an “imitation” of it—however convincing. Much attention is therefore on whether AI can really be empathic at all. Many maintain that it cannot. This may very well be true. Can a system that has never felt anything have empathy? This is an irresolvable debate about the nature of minds and what we take empathy to mean. Instead, this paper argues for asking patients to rate how empathic responses feel on a 1–5 scale—a judgement only they can make. Their ratings let researchers test which design features raise perceived empathy and whether responses that score highly are also accurate, safe and helpful.

Abstract

This paper focuses on a central question for Human-AI interaction: Can you be friends with an AI agent? If not, why not? Some have argued that friendship with AI agents is impossible because software artifacts do not, and cannot, care about you. Proponents of human–machine friendships have responded that such relationships may indeed be one-sided, but still count as relationships of genuine love and affection—perhaps constituting a whole new category of friendship. Our paper takes a different path. We argue that you cannot be friends with an AI agent because you cannot sensibly be a friend to an AI agent. Being a friend to an AI would require caring about the good of the AI agent for its own sake, and it does not make sense to care about an AI agent in that way, since these agents lack a good of their own . After spelling out this argument, and responding to several objections, we highlight some initial implications of our argument, the most important of which is that the very idea of a tool – or, technological fix – to address social isolation and loneliness is misguided.

Four in ten patients in England’s NHS hospitals do not always feel able to talk to staff about their worries and fears. Successive inquiries have found patients dismissed when they asked for help and even told to “get a grip”. Empathy in healthcare involves attending to what the patient may be feeling or worrying about, trying to understand what the situation is like for them, then responding in words and actions shaped by that understanding. Its absence can cause avoidable harm. Talking to patients is now partly AI’s job. One chatbot has delivered nearly 650,000 assessments for NHS Talking Therapies. Robots are arriving on hospital wards, where one has been used to ease children’s anxiety during radiotherapy. Both are jobs usually done by healthcare staff. AI does not experience the fatigue or impatience that structural pressures can cause, but how it communicates with patients raises design concerns. So what can researchers establish about empathy in AI’s exchanges with patients? Research in affective computing and human–robot interaction often takes a functional view of empathy: can a system detect emotion and adapt its response? However, there is often more at stake in healthcare than in many other settings. Some people who interact with AI will be frightened, seriously ill, or trying to understand what a diagnosis means for their future. Even routine or informational exchanges may feel cold or brusque. Empathy is often considered a cornerstone of good healthcare, and some argue that it must be rooted in genuine care, not an “imitation” of it—however convincing. - IEEE Xplore 那条带"Index Terms: Genuine Care"的 Replika 检索结果，我**只拿到搜索页链接与供应商标引摘录，没有读到该论文本身**，故不列为证据。
- 没有中文数据库（CNKI 等）渠道，也没有做系统综述式检索，因此不能声称这是该议题近五年的完整图景。
